topics.title: Relater un événement passé
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to state the difference between passé composé and imparfait.
The students should be able to explain the use of temporal adverbs in French.
The students should be able to form sentences using passé composé and imparfait correctly.

Introduction:
We have learned how to talk about our daily activities in French. Today we will learn how to talk about events that happened in the past, like when you went to the market last weekend or when your school had a cultural festival.

Content:
The passé composé is used to talk about completed actions in the past. It is formed with the auxiliary verb avoir or être and the past participle of the main verb. For example, "J'ai mangé" means "I ate". The imparfait is used to describe ongoing actions or states in the past. It is formed by adding specific endings to the stem of the verb. For example, "Je mangeais" means "I was eating". Temporal adverbs help us situate actions in time. Common ones include "hier" (yesterday), "la semaine dernière" (last week), "l'année dernière" (last year), and "il y a" (ago). In Nigerian context, you might say "Hier, j'ai acheté du poisson au marché" (Yesterday, I bought fish at the market) or "L'année dernière, nous avions une fête culturelle à l'école" (Last year, we had a cultural festival at school).

Class activity:
Students will work in pairs to create a short dialogue about their weekend activities, using both passé composé and imparfait. They will then present their dialogue to the class.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is the difference between passé composé and imparfait?
2. Form a sentence using "hier" and passé composé.
3. Explain when you would use imparfait instead of passé composé.
4. Translate "I was eating rice when my friend arrived" into French.

Summary:
Today we learned how to talk about past events in French using passé composé, imparfait, and temporal adverbs to situate our actions in time.

topics.title: Rapporter un fait récent
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to construct sentences using "venir de" with passé composé.
The students should be able to identify other structures used to express recent past actions.
The students should be able to differentiate between immediate past and distant past in French.

Introduction:
Last week we learned how to talk about past events in general. Today we will focus on very recent actions, like what you did just a few minutes ago or earlier this morning, which is common in everyday conversations.

Content:
The structure "venir de" + infinitive is used to express actions that have just been completed. It is always followed by the present tense of "venir" and the infinitive of the main verb. For example, "Je viens de manger" means "I have just eaten". Other structures for expressing recent actions include "à l'instant" (just now), "tout à l'heure" (a little while ago), and "il y a un instant" (a moment ago). In Nigerian context, you might say "Je viens d'arriver de l'école" (I have just come from school) or "Il vient de téléphoner à sa mère" (He has just called his mother). These structures help emphasize the immediacy of the action.

Class activity:
Students will create a short news report about recent events in the school using the "venir de" structure and other expressions of recent past. They will present their reports to the class.

Evaluation questions:
1. How do you form the immediate past in French?
2. Translate "She has just left" into French.
3. Name two other expressions besides "venir de" that can be used for recent past.
4. When would you use "venir de" instead of passé composé alone?

Summary:
Today we learned how to report very recent actions in French using "venir de" and other temporal expressions that emphasize immediacy.

topics.title: Comprendre un récit / Écrire son journal journal intime.
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to understand the main points of a simple French narrative.
The students should be able to identify key vocabulary related to daily life in French narratives.
The students should be able to write a short personal diary entry in French.

Introduction:
We have learned how to talk about past events. Now we will practice understanding stories written in French and also learn how to write our own personal diary entries, which is useful for practicing our French writing skills.

Content:
When reading a French narrative, look for key information such as characters, setting, and sequence of events. Pay attention to verb tenses used and how they indicate when actions happened. Common vocabulary in daily life narratives includes words for family members, food, activities, and places. For example, "ma famille" (my family), "le petit déjeuner" (breakfast), "aller à l'école" (go to school). When writing a personal diary, use first person perspective and past tense to describe your day. Include your feelings and thoughts. For example, "Aujourd'hui, je suis allé(e) au marché avec ma mère. Nous avons acheté des légumes pour la soupe. J'étais content(e) parce que j'aime aider à la cuisine." In Nigerian context, you might write about going to a local market, helping with cooking traditional Nigerian food, or attending a family gathering.

Class activity:
Students will read a short French narrative about a child's day and then write their own diary entry about their weekend, using vocabulary and structures they have learned.

Evaluation questions:
1. What are three important elements to look for when reading a French narrative?
2. Write a sentence about what you ate yesterday in French.
3. How would you say "I was happy" in French in a diary entry?
4. What tense is typically used in personal diary entries?

Summary:
Today we practiced reading French narratives and learned how to write personal diary entries in French to express our daily experiences and feelings.

topics.title: Dire ce que l'on va faire
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to form sentences using the futur proche in French.
The students should be able to construct sentences using the futur simple.
The students should be able to differentiate between futur proche and futur simple.

Introduction:
We have learned how to talk about past events. Now we will learn how to talk about future plans and intentions, which is very useful when discussing what you will do during the holidays or your goals for the next school year.

Content:
The futur proche is used to talk about immediate future plans and is formed with the present tense of "aller" + infinitive. For example, "Je vais manger" means "I am going to eat". It is commonly used for plans that will happen soon. The futur simple is used to talk about future actions that will happen later and is formed by adding specific endings to the infinitive of the verb. For example, "Je mangerai" means "I will eat". It is used for more distant future or intentions. In Nigerian context, you might say "Je vais aller à la plage ce week-end" (I am going to the beach this weekend) for immediate plans or "J'étudierai à l'université l'année prochaine" (I will study at university next year) for future intentions. Common expressions of future time include "demain" (tomorrow), "la semaine prochaine" (next week), and "l'année prochaine" (next year).

Class activity:
Students will create a dialogue between two friends planning their holidays, using both futur proche and futur simple to discuss their immediate and future plans.

Evaluation questions:
1. How do you form the futur proche in French?
2. When would you use futur simple instead of futur proche?
3. Translate "I will visit my grandmother next month" into French.
4. Give an example sentence using "demain" and futur proche.

Summary:
Today we learned how to talk about future plans in French using both futur proche for immediate plans and futur simple for more distant future intentions.

topics.title: Midterm Examination
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to demonstrate their understanding of the topics covered in the first half of the term.
The students should be able to apply the grammar structures and vocabulary learned in various contexts.

Introduction:
Today we will have our midterm examination to assess your understanding of the French topics we have covered so far this term. This will help me know which areas we need to focus on more in our future lessons.

Content:
The midterm examination will cover all the topics we have studied this term, including talking about past events using passé composé and imparfait, reporting recent facts with "venir de", understanding narratives, and discussing future plans with futur proche and futur simple. The exam will consist of different sections such as vocabulary matching, grammar exercises, reading comprehension, and writing a short paragraph. Remember to manage your time well and read each question carefully before answering. In Nigerian context, the exam might include questions about daily Nigerian life, such as describing a typical market day or talking about traditional festivals using the grammar structures we have learned.

Class activity:
The midterm examination will be conducted under examination conditions. Students will work individually to complete all sections of the exam within the allotted time.

Evaluation questions:
The midterm examination will contain various question types including:
1. Matching French vocabulary with English equivalents.
2. Fill in the blanks with correct verb forms (passé composé, imparfait, futur proche, futur simple).
3. Complete sentences with appropriate temporal adverbs.
4. Read a short French passage and answer comprehension questions.
5. Write a short paragraph (50-80 words) about your weekend plans using futur proche and futur simple.

Summary:
The midterm examination will assess your understanding of all French topics covered so far this term, providing valuable feedback on your progress and areas for improvement.

topics.title: Faire des projets
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to express personal and school projects using appropriate future tenses.
The students should be able to use vocabulary related to planning and projects in French.
The students should be able to write a simple project proposal in French.

Introduction:
After our midterm break, we will focus on discussing projects and plans for the future. This is important not only for academic purposes but also for expressing your personal goals and intentions in French.

Content:
When discussing projects, we use the futur simple to express intentions and plans that will be realized in the future. Vocabulary related to planning includes "projeter" (to plan), "préparer" (to prepare), "organiser" (to organize), "commencer" (to start), and "terminer" (to finish). For example, "Je projeterai de lire plus de livres français" means "I plan to read more French books". When writing a project proposal, include the following elements: title, objective, materials needed, steps to follow, and expected outcome. For example, "Mon projet: Apprendre à cuisiner un plat nigérian. Objectif: Préparer le riz et la sauce pour ma famille. Matériaux: Riz, légumes, épices. Étapes: Acheter les ingrédients, Préparer les légumes, Faire cuire le riz, Préparer la sauce. Résultat: Ma famille pourra déguster un bon repas." Common time expressions for projects include "d'ici la fin du mois" (by the end of the month), "l'année prochaine" (next year), and "d'ici la fin de l'année" (by the end of the year).

Class activity:
Students will work in groups to create a project proposal for improving their classroom or school. They will write a short proposal in French and present it to the class, explaining their plan using appropriate future tenses and vocabulary.

Evaluation questions:
1. How do you say "I plan to" in French?
2. Name three vocabulary words related to planning projects.
3. What are the four main elements of a project proposal?
4. Translate "We will start the project next week" into French.

Summary:
Today we learned how to express future projects and plans in French using appropriate vocabulary and future tenses, which will help you communicate your intentions clearly.

topics.title: Midterm Break
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to rest and recharge for the second half of the term.
The students should be able to review previously learned material informally.

Introduction:
This is our midterm break, a time to rest from your studies and prepare for the remaining part of the term. Use this time wisely to relax and also review what we have learned so far.

Content:
During this midterm break, you should take time to rest and engage in activities that help you relax and recharge your mind. This could include spending time with family, reading books, playing sports, or pursuing hobbies. You might also consider reviewing the French topics we have covered this term, such as passé composé, imparfait, "venir de", futur proche, and futur simple. You could practice by writing short diary entries in French about your break activities or by talking with family members about your future plans. Remember that consistent practice, even during breaks, helps maintain and improve your language skills. In Nigerian context, you might use this time to visit local markets, attend cultural events, or help with family activities while practicing your French vocabulary related to these experiences.

Class activity:
No formal class activity during the midterm break. However, students are encouraged to keep a simple French journal of their break activities to practice their writing skills.

Evaluation questions:
There will be no formal evaluation during the midterm break. However, you should be prepared to discuss what you did during your break when classes resume.

Summary:
The midterm break is an important time for rest and informal review of previously learned material, helping you return to classes refreshed and ready to continue your French studies.
